title: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ κροκόδειλος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 35. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ κροκόδειλος περὶ εὐγενείας ἤριζον.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx kai krokodeilos peri eugeneias ērizon.
sentences.l: A fox and a crocodile were quarrelling about good birth.
sentences.n: εὐγένεια is birth into a good family — the pedigree a Greek gentleman boasted of. The imperfect ἤριζον sets the quarrel going rather than finishing it; these fables regularly open with an imperfect scene and then fire aorists at it.

sentences.t: Πολλὰ δὲ τοῦ κροκοδείλου διεξιόντος περὶ τῆς τῶν προγόνων λαμπρότητος καὶ τὸ τελευταῖον λέγοντος ὡς γεγυμνασιαρχηκότων ἐστὶ πατέρων, ἡ ἀλώπηξ ἔφη· « Ἀλλὰ κἂν σὺ μὴ εἴπῃς, ἀπὸ τοῦ δέρματος φαίνῃ ὅτι ἀπὸ πολλῶν ἐτῶν εἶ γεγυμνασμένος. »
sentences.tr: Polla de tou krokodeilou diexiontos peri tēs tōn progonōn lamprotētos kai to teleutaion legontos hōs gegymnasiarchēkotōn esti paterōn, hē alōpēx ephē· « Alla kan sy mē eipēis, apo tou dermatos phainēi hoti apo pollōn etōn ei gegymnasmenos. »
sentences.l: And the crocodile going through many things about the splendour of his ancestors, and at the last saying that he is of fathers who have held the gymnasiarchy, the fox said: « But even if you should not say it, from your hide you are plainly seen to have been exercised for many years. »
sentences.i: The crocodile held forth at length on the lustre of his ancestors, and ended by saying that his fathers had been gymnasiarchs; whereupon the fox said, “Even if you said nothing, your hide makes it plain that you have been well exercised for many years.”
sentences.n: The joke is a pun on two words from one root. γεγυμνασιαρχηκότων is from γυμνασιαρχεῖν, to serve as gymnasiarch — the wealthy citizen who paid for a city's gymnasium, an office worth boasting of; γεγυμνασμένος means only “exercised, put through training,” and said of a hide it points at wear and battering. τοῦ κροκοδείλου διεξιόντος … λέγοντος is a genitive absolute: a noun and its participle standing free of the main clause to set the scene (“while the crocodile was going through…”). κἂν is a crasis of καὶ ἐάν, “even if,” and takes the subjunctive εἴπῃς. φαίνῃ is second person middle-passive — “you are seen to be, you show plain”; the crocodile himself is its subject, not an impersonal “it is clear.”

sentences.t: Οὕτως καὶ τῶν ψευδολόγων ἀνθρώπων ἔλεγχός ἐστι τὰ πράγματα.
sentences.tr: Houtōs kai tōn pseudologōn anthrōpōn elenchos esti ta pragmata.
sentences.l: So too of men who speak falsely the refutation is the facts.
sentences.i: So too, the facts are the refutation of men who deal in lies.
sentences.n: ἔλεγχος is the courtroom word for cross-examination and the proof it yields. τὰ πράγματα, “the things, the realities,” is the subject and ἔλεγχος the predicate: nobody has to argue with a liar, the state of affairs does it.
